subject: Naturkunskap 1b
title: Body and health
sourceSummary: What affects health (lifestyle, environment and heredity), sexual health and relationships at an adult level, drugs and addiction, and public health as a concept.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the determinants of health?
questions.opener: Think broadly — it's about more than just lifestyle choices like diet and exercise.
choices: The factors, e.g. lifestyle habits, environment, heredity, and social and economic conditions, that together affect the health of an individual or a population
Only the genes one has inherited from one's parents
Another word for the healthcare resources in a region
Only how much one exercises each week
questions.explanation: The determinants of health cover a broad spectrum: lifestyle habits (diet, exercise, sleep, drugs), heredity, environmental factors and social/economic conditions such as education and income. Looking only at genes or only at exercise misses how many factors interact.

questions.prompt: Why are socioeconomic factors, such as level of education and income, often linked to differences in health between different groups in society?
questions.opener: Think about what things like income and education can affect indirectly, such as housing, eating habits and access to healthcare.
choices: Socioeconomic factors have no link to health according to research
They affect, among other things, access to good housing, healthy food, education about health and access to healthcare, which in turn can affect health outcomes
Only genetic differences explain all health differences between groups
The link only applies in low-income countries
questions.explanation: Research consistently shows links between socioeconomic status and health: higher income and education are often associated with a better living environment, more knowledge of healthy choices and easier access to healthcare, which contributes to better health outcomes on average. This applies to varying degrees in many countries, not only low-income countries.

questions.prompt: What does consent mean in a sexual relationship?
questions.opener: Think about how consent must be current, voluntary, and able to be withdrawn.
choices: That a person saying yes once means consent applies forever
That both parties voluntarily and knowingly agree to what is happening, and that consent can be withdrawn at any time
That it is enough for one party to assume the other wants to
That consent is only needed in committed relationships, not in casual encounters
questions.explanation: Consent must be voluntary, clear and apply to the specific situation at hand — it can always be withdrawn, and it applies regardless of relationship status. A previous yes does not automatically mean yes in a different situation, and merely assuming consent is not enough.

questions.prompt: Which is the only common form of contraception that both reduces the risk of pregnancy and protects against most sexually transmitted infections (STIs)?
questions.opener: Think about which method of contraception acts as a physical barrier between bodily fluids.
choices: The pill
Condom
IUD (coil)
Contraceptive implant
questions.explanation: The condom acts as a barrier that prevents direct contact between bodily fluids and therefore protects against both pregnancy and most sexually transmitted infections. Hormonal methods such as the pill, the IUD and the contraceptive implant protect against pregnancy but not against STIs.

questions.prompt: What characterises a physical dependence on a drug, e.g. alcohol or nicotine?
questions.opener: Think about what happens in the body if the person suddenly stops using the drug.
choices: That the person only feels a psychological craving for the drug, with no bodily reactions
That the body has adapted to the drug so that withdrawal symptoms, e.g. shaking or nausea, occur when use stops
That the dependence automatically disappears after a week without the drug
That only young people can develop physical dependence
questions.explanation: Physical dependence means the body has adapted its functioning to the drug's presence, so that withdrawal symptoms (e.g. shaking, sweating, nausea) occur when use is reduced or stopped. This differs from purely psychological dependence, which involves a strong craving without the same bodily withdrawal, but both forms can occur at the same time.

questions.prompt: What is meant by public health, as distinct from an individual's own health?
questions.opener: Think about which level the concept operates at — a person, or an entire population.
choices: Another word for the organisation of healthcare services
The state of health and its distribution across an entire population, along with the efforts made to improve and even out health in society
Only how many people are on sick leave at a given time
A measure of one individual's fitness
questions.explanation: Public health concerns the state of health of an entire population or group, including how health is distributed between different groups, as well as the preventive and health-promoting work (public health work) carried out to improve and even out health. It is therefore a broader, societal perspective than a single individual's state of health.

questions.prompt: Using an example, explain how lifestyle, environment and heredity can interact to affect the risk of developing a lifestyle-related disease, e.g. type 2 diabetes.
questions.opener: Imagine a person with a hereditary risk of the disease — what determines whether the risk is actually realised?
questions.answer: Genetic vulnerability increases the risk of type 2 diabetes but rarely determines alone whether the disease develops; environmental factors and lifestyle habits, such as access to healthy food, physical activity and stress levels, interact with heredity and together determine how great the actual risk becomes for a given individual.
steps: Some people have a hereditary (genetic) vulnerability that makes the body's insulin sensitivity more easily disrupted — this gives an elevated baseline risk for type 2 diabetes.
The environment a person lives in, e.g. access to healthy and affordable food and opportunities for physical activity nearby, affects which choices are easy to make day to day.
Lifestyle habits such as diet, physical activity, sleep and stress management then directly affect the body's metabolism and weight.
Socioeconomic conditions, such as income, working hours and education, often indirectly govern both the environment and which lifestyle habits are realistic to maintain.

The end result is that disease risk rarely depends on a single factor, but arises from the interplay between heredity, environment and lifestyle together — which is why preventive work at several levels (individual and society) matters.

questions.prompt: Summarise the key points about the determinants of health, sexual health, drugs and addiction, and public health.
questions.opener: Go through what affects health, what is required for a safe relationship, and what distinguishes the individual and population levels.
questions.answer: Determinants of health: lifestyle habits, heredity, environment and socioeconomic conditions interact and affect health · Consent: must be voluntary, clear, apply to the current situation, and be able to be withdrawn at any time · Contraception: the condom is the only common method that protects against both pregnancy and most sexually transmitted infections; hormonal methods such as the pill only protect against pregnancy · Physical dependence: the body has adapted to the drug, withdrawal occurs when use stops · Psychological dependence: a strong craving for the drug without the same bodily withdrawal · Public health: the state of health and its distribution across an entire population, along with the preventive work done to improve and even out health in society.

questions.prompt: What is meant by "health-promoting" work, as distinct from purely disease-preventive work?
questions.opener: Think about the difference between building up something positive and merely preventing something negative.
choices: Actively strengthening factors that contribute to good health and well-being, e.g. by creating good conditions for physical activity and social settings, rather than solely preventing specific diseases
Another word for only treating diseases that have already occurred
A concept that applies only within healthcare, not in schools or workplaces
That health-promoting work is always more expensive than disease-preventive work
questions.explanation: Health-promoting work is about actively strengthening factors that contribute to well-being, e.g. through safe social settings and opportunities for physical activity, rather than focusing solely on preventing specific diseases.

questions.prompt: What is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) that is often asymptomatic but, if untreated, can lead to infertility?
questions.opener: Think of a very common STI among young people that often produces no clear symptoms at all.
choices: Chlamydia
The common cold
Influenza
Chickenpox
questions.explanation: Chlamydia is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections and is often asymptomatic, but if left untreated can lead to complications such as infertility, especially in women.

questions.prompt: What characterises an equal and healthy relationship?
questions.opener: Think about what characterises a relationship where both parties feel safe and respected.
choices: Mutual respect, open communication, and both parties' boundaries and wishes being taken seriously
That one party always decides for the other
That conflicts may never be expressed openly
That both parties must agree on absolutely everything
questions.explanation: An equal and healthy relationship is characterised by mutual respect, open communication, and both parties' boundaries and wishes being taken seriously - not by one party always deciding or conflicts never being allowed to surface.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between risky use and dependence on alcohol?
questions.opener: Think about whether HOW MUCH one drinks alone determines whether one is dependent.
choices: Risky use is a level of consumption that increases the risk of harm without the person necessarily being dependent, while dependence involves a strong, often uncontrollable urge to continue using despite negative consequences
Risky use and dependence mean exactly the same thing
Dependence is always less serious than risky use
Risky use can only apply to drugs, never to alcohol
questions.explanation: Risky use refers to a level of consumption that increases the risk of harm without the person necessarily being dependent, while dependence involves a strong, often uncontrollable urge to continue despite negative consequences - so a person can engage in risky use without being dependent.

questions.prompt: How do many addictive drugs affect the brain's reward system?
questions.opener: Think about which neurotransmitter is often linked to feelings of reward and pleasure.
choices: They increase the release of the neurotransmitter dopamine, producing a feeling of pleasure that the body can learn to seek repeatedly
They shut down the brain's reward system entirely and permanently
They affect only the muscles, never the brain
They have no connection at all to brain chemistry
questions.explanation: Many addictive drugs increase the release of dopamine in the brain's reward system, producing a feeling of pleasure that the brain can learn to seek repeatedly, which contributes to the development of addiction.

questions.prompt: What is an example of a structural public health measure, as distinct from a measure aimed at a single individual?
questions.opener: Think about the difference between a measure aimed at a single person and one that automatically affects the whole population.
choices: Legislation on smoke-free public environments, which reduces exposure to secondhand smoke across the entire population
An individual doctor giving dietary advice to a patient
A person deciding on their own to quit smoking
One friend giving another friend advice about exercise
questions.explanation: Legislation on smoke-free public environments is a structural public health measure because it automatically affects the whole population's exposure to secondhand smoke, unlike individual measures such as dietary advice given to a single patient.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a public health indicator used to track a population's health over time?
questions.opener: Think of a measure that describes the health of an entire population, not a single person.
choices: Average life expectancy in the population
An individual's blood pressure at a doctor's visit
The number of rooms in a person's home
A person's favourite food
questions.explanation: Average life expectancy is a common public health indicator used to track and compare populations' health over time and between different groups. An individual's blood pressure instead says something about that person's own health, not about public health as a whole.
